text:
Then Hannah prayed:
"My heart exults in the LORD;
in the LORD my horn is lifted high.
My mouth speaks boldly against my enemies,
for I rejoice in your salvation.

versions.text:
Then Hannah prayed:
"My heart exults in the LORD;
in the LORD my strength is lifted high.
My mouth speaks boldly against my enemies,
for I rejoice in your salvation.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew 'my horn' (קרני) is rendered figuratively as 'strength' here, but the same image is kept literally in verse 10 ('lift high the horn of his anointed'). Keeping 'horn' here preserves the poetic inclusio of the song and makes the two verses consistent; a footnote can explain that the horn symbolizes strength and dignity.

text:
The bows of the mighty are broken,
but the weak are armed with strength.

Those who were full now hire themselves out for bread,
but the hungry go hungry no more.
Even the barren woman has borne seven,
but she who had many sons is left desolate.

versions.text:
Those who were full now hire themselves out for bread,
but the hungry go hungry no more.
The barren woman has borne seven,
but she who had many sons is left desolate.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew particle עַד here carries the sense 'even' (the climactic reversal). Including it strengthens the contrast and matches the rhetorical force of the line.

text:
The LORD brings death and gives life;
he brings down to Sheol and raises up.

versions.text:
The LORD brings death and gives life;
he brings down to the grave and raises up.
versions.explanation: 'Sheol' is the named realm of the dead rather than a burial place; using the name (with a brief footnote explaining it as the place of the dead) avoids narrowing the imagery to a physical grave.

text:
The LORD makes poor and makes rich;
he humbles and he exalts.

He raises the poor from the dust
and lifts the needy from the ash heap,
seating them among princes
and giving them a throne of honor.
For the foundations of the earth are the LORD's,
and on them he has set the world.

He guards the steps of his faithful ones,
but the wicked are silenced in darkness—
for no one prevails by his own strength.
Then Elkanah went home to Ramah, but the boy remained to serve the LORD under Eli the priest.
Eli's sons were worthless men; they had no regard for the LORD.
This was their practice with the people: whenever anyone offered a sacrifice, the priest's servant would come with a three-pronged fork in his hand while the meat was boiling.
He would thrust it into the pan or kettle or cauldron or pot, and whatever the fork brought up the priest took for himself. This is how they treated all the Israelites who came to Shiloh.
Even before the fat was burned, the priest's servant would come and say to the man who was sacrificing, "Give the priest meat to roast. He will not take boiled meat from you—only raw."
If the man said to him, "Let the fat be burned first, then take whatever you want," the servant would answer, "No, hand it over now; if you won't, I'll take it by force."
So the sin of these young men was very great in the LORD's sight, for they treated the offering of the LORD with contempt.
But Samuel served before the LORD, a boy wearing a linen ephod.
Each year his mother made him a little robe and brought it to him when she went up with her husband to offer the yearly sacrifice.
Eli would bless Elkanah and his wife, saying, "May the LORD give you children by this woman in place of the one asked for and given to the LORD." Then they would return home.

versions.text: Eli would bless Elkanah and his wife, saying, "May the LORD give you children by this woman in place of the one she asked of him and gave to him." Then they would return home.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew says 'in place of the petition that was asked for the LORD'; the current wording adds 'she asked of him and gave to him', assigning the asking to Hannah (the verb is masculine) and adding a second clause not in the text. A more neutral rendering keeps the interpretive sense of dedication without adding an unsupported subject.

text: And the LORD showed his care for Hannah: she conceived and bore three sons and two daughters. Meanwhile the boy Samuel grew up in the presence of the LORD.
Now Eli was very old, and he kept hearing about everything his sons were doing to all Israel and how they slept with the women who served at the entrance to the tent of meeting.
So he said to them, "Why do you do such things? I hear about your evil deeds from all these people.

versions.text: So he said to them, "Why do you do such things? From all the people I hear of your evil deeds.
versions.explanation: The fronted phrase 'From all the people' is awkward for oral reading and obscures the emphasis; the natural English order follows the Hebrew sense ('I keep hearing... from all these people') and flows better when read aloud.

text: No, my sons; the report I hear is not good. You are leading the LORD's people into sin.

If one person sins against another, God may mediate for him; but if someone sins against the LORD, who will intercede for him?" His sons, however, would not listen to their father, for it was the LORD's will to put them to death.
And the boy Samuel continued to grow, and he was pleasing both to the LORD and to the people.
A man of God came to Eli and said to him, "This is what the LORD says: Did I not reveal myself plainly to your father's house when they were in Egypt under Pharaoh?

Out of all the tribes of Israel I chose your father to be my priest, to go up to my altar, to burn incense, and to wear the ephod before me. And I gave your father's house all the offerings made by fire by the Israelites.

Why then do you trample on my sacrifice and my offering, which I commanded for my dwelling? You honor your sons above me, fattening yourselves on the choicest part of every offering my people Israel bring.

Therefore the LORD, the God of Israel, declares: I did indeed promise that your house and your father's house would minister before me forever. But now the LORD declares: Far be it from me! Those who honor me I will honor, but those who despise me will be treated with contempt.
The days are coming when I will cut off your strength and the strength of your father's house, and no one in your family will live to old age.
You will look on in distress at my dwelling. Though good will be done for Israel, never again will there be an old man in your house.
Every one of your line whom I do not cut off from my altar will be spared only to wear out your eyes with weeping and to grieve your heart, and all your descendants will die in the prime of life.
And this will be the sign to you: what happens to your two sons, Hophni and Phinehas—both of them will die on the same day.
Then I will raise up for myself a faithful priest, who will do what is in my heart and mind. I will build him an enduring house, and he will walk before my anointed one all his days.

versions.text: Then I will raise up for myself a faithful priest, who will do what is in my heart and mind. I will build a lasting house for him, and he will minister before my anointed one always.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew verb הִתְהַלֵּךְ means 'walk about, live/conduct oneself'; 'minister' narrows it to cultic service and adds an idea not in the text. 'Walk before' preserves the covenant idiom and reads well aloud. Also, 'all his days' renders כָּל־הַיָּמִים more naturally than 'always,' and 'an enduring house' keeps the parallel with 'faithful priest' (both נֶאֱמָן) without the slightly flat 'lasting house for him.'

text: And everyone left in your house will come and bow down before him for a piece of silver and a loaf of bread, and will say, 'Please attach me to one of the priestly offices, so I may eat a morsel of bread.'"

versions.text: And everyone left in your house will come and bow down before him for a piece of silver and a loaf of bread, pleading, 'Appoint me to some priestly office, so I may have a morsel of bread to eat.'"
versions.explanation: The Hebrew simply says 'and he will say,' and the verb סְפָחֵנִי means 'attach/join me,' a humble request for a place rather than a formal appointment; the particle נָא ('please') is currently unrepresented. The revised wording is closer to the Hebrew and still flows naturally when read aloud.
